common_name: Invincibelle Lace Hydrangea (Plum-Purple Lacecap Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Invincibelle Lace was the first smooth hydrangea introduced with lacecap flowers in plum and purple tones rather than the pink or white typical of the Invincibelle series.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Invincibelle Lace is a Proven Winners selection of native smooth hydrangea distinguished by lacecap flower heads that open with pale pink outer bracts surrounding a mass of tiny plum-purple fertile florets, a color combination not found in other smooth hydrangea cultivars. Strong, upright dark red stems hold the flowers well without flopping. Like other smooth hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter and still flower reliably the same season. Its looser, more open habit and unusual color suit informal, cottage, and wildlife plantings, and the flowers attract bees and butterflies through a long summer-into-fall bloom season.

common_name: Invincibelle Garnetta Hydrangea (Compact Garnet-Pink Reblooming Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Invincibelle Garnetta is a compact, reblooming selection of native smooth hydrangea with deep garnet-pink to burgundy mophead flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Invincibelle Garnetta is a compact Proven Winners smooth hydrangea selection bearing rounded mophead flowers that open rich pink and deepen toward a dark garnet or burgundy tone, among the deepest flower colors in the Invincibelle series. Its naturally dense, rounded habit stays smaller than most smooth hydrangeas, fitting foundation plantings and small borders without pruning. It blooms on new wood and reblooms over a long season from summer into fall; cut back hard in late winter for the strongest flush of flowering stems.

common_name: Tiara Mountain Hydrangea (Compact Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Tiara is a low, compact mountain hydrangea selection named for the ring of showy sterile florets encircling each lacecap flower head like a small crown.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Tiara is a dwarf, low-mounding mountain hydrangea selection bearing lacecap flower heads in blue to pink tones depending on soil pH, with a neat ring of showier sterile florets around the center that gives the cultivar its name. Its compact, tidy habit suits small gardens, foundation plantings, and the front of a shaded border, and the foliage takes on attractive reddish-purple tones in cooler autumn weather. Like other mountain hydrangeas, it is generally more cold-hardy and sun-tolerant than bigleaf hydrangea. Water regularly during dry spells and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat.

common_name: Shichidanka Mountain Hydrangea (Komachi Double Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Shichidanka (also sold as Komachi) is a Japanese heirloom mountain hydrangea prized for its unusual fully double, star-shaped lacecap florets.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Shichidanka is a slow-growing, long-cultivated Japanese mountain hydrangea noted for its unusual fully double, star-shaped sterile florets ringing each lacecap flower head, in shades of pink to lavender-blue that shift with soil pH the same way bigleaf hydrangea does. It is also sold under the name Komachi. Give it a sheltered woodland-edge setting, keep soil consistently moist, and limit pruning to removing spent flower heads, since this cultivar is more deliberate in its growth than many mountain hydrangea selections.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Woodlander was selected from seed collected in Korea and introduced to cultivation by Woodlanders Nursery.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Woodlander is a compact Korean mountain hydrangea selection with green foliage that develops varying degrees of purple tones through the growing season, most pronounced in a sun-drenched spot early in the year, paired with classic lacecap flower heads in blue to pink tones through summer. Its Korean provenance and compact habit make it a good choice for a shaded native-plant or woodland-edge border. Water regularly during dry spells and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog in partial shade in spring; Poisson's primrose, native to wet montane meadows of Sichuan and Yunnan, must have constant moisture through the growing season.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade beside streams, ponds, or bog gardens. Poisson's primrose is a semi-evergreen candelabra-type species from western China, sending up stems bearing several whorls of fragrant, magenta-pink to carmine flowers with a small yellow eye in summer, blooming somewhat later than many other candelabra primroses. It self-sows in consistently damp ground and combines well with other candelabra species such as Primula bulleyana and Primula beesiana along a shaded pond or streamside planting. It dies back if soil dries out even briefly during active growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog in partial shade in spring; moonlight primrose, native to damp alpine meadows of Tibet and Bhutan, needs reliably moist, organic-rich soil.

directions: Plant divisions in fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade beside a stream, pond, or bog garden. Moonlight primrose sends up stems dusted with pale mealy farina, topped with a loose, nodding, fragrant cluster of bell-shaped flowers that open cream, yellow, or mauve to deep purple depending on the form. Its soft coloring and fragrance make it a good companion for candelabra primroses and moisture-loving ferns at a damp woodland pond margin. Keep soil consistently moist; it is not fussy about soil pH as long as moisture is reliable.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog in shade to partial shade in spring; this Bhutanese candelabra primrose is one of the earliest of the group to flower each season.

directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade at a stream, pond, or bog margin. Chungensis primrose is a candelabra-type species from Bhutan, opening red buds into whorls of apricot-orange flowers stacked up slender stems in early summer, among the first candelabra primroses to bloom each year. Its warm orange coloring is a useful contrast to the pinks, purples, and crimsons of other candelabra species such as Primula bulleyana and Primula pulverulenta when planted together at a woodland pond edge. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season; it will not tolerate drying out.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade in fall or early spring; Gold-Laced Group is a historic English florists' strain grown true to type by division of named clones, since seed-grown plants vary in quality.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in bright partial shade. Gold-Laced Group is a centuries-old English polyanthus strain, prized by Georgian and Victorian florists as a competitive show flower, bearing small, flat flowers in dark maroon, mahogany, or near-black with a narrow gold or silver edge around each petal and a bright yellow eye. The crinkled green rosettes are long-lived where summers are not too hot. Divide congested clumps after flowering to maintain the strain's distinctive lacing true to type, since seed-raised plants are variable.
